cues.text: Let yourself settle now. Bring your attention to your breathing. Take one comfortably deep breath in, without straining. Then let it go gently. Allow the next breath to find its own rhythm, while your shoulders begin to soften.
Take a moment to adjust your position if you need to. Let your hands rest where they feel comfortable. Your eyes may close, or remain softly open. There is no right way to look relaxed.

Feel where your body meets the surface beneath you. You do not have to carry all of your weight. Let that support receive a little more of you as you breathe out, keeping your position comfortable and easy.
Follow the small movement of your breathing. Let it arrive naturally, without trying to fill your lungs or hold your breath. A comfortable breath is enough.
Choose one place where breathing is simple to notice. Perhaps the air at your nose, the movement of your ribs, or the gentle rise and fall of your abdomen. Stay with that one place for this breath.
Notice where you feel this breath most clearly: around the nostrils, in the ribs, or in the belly. Let that simple sensation bring you back to the present.

Notice the beginning of an inhalation. Follow its movement without pulling in extra air. Notice the moment it turns into an exhalation. Follow that breath out, allowing the change of direction to happen by itself.

Let your attention travel with one complete breath, from its first small movement to its natural end. There is no special depth to reach. Let the breath be ordinary, and let your attention be kind and unhurried.
Return to the breath. Relax the jaw, soften the eyes, and allow the shoulders to move a little farther away from the ears.

As the next breath comes in, silently think, arriving. As it leaves, silently think, softening. You need not say the words aloud. Let them sit lightly beside the breathing, without making your breath fit the words.

Feel the space around your eyes. Allow your brow to become smooth, if that feels natural. Notice whether your jaw is holding anything. With your next easy exhalation, give the muscles of your face permission to do less.
Bring awareness to the forehead and the small muscles around the eyes. Let the face become less busy. Allow a little space between the teeth and let the tongue rest easily.

Bring your attention back to the ribs. You may feel movement at the sides, at the front, or towards your back. There is room for the breath to move in whichever direction feels easiest in this position.
Notice the ribs moving gently as you breathe. Let the movement be small if that is comfortable. There is no need to pull in the abdomen or make the breath deeper than it wants to be.
Now try a simple count, only if it feels comfortable. At the end of your next out breath, silently count one. At the end of the following out breath, count two. Keep your breathing at its own pace.

Continue gently to three, then four, then five, counting only when each breath has finished. There is no need to make the breaths longer or to wait between them. Let the numbers follow you, rather than lead you.

If you lose your place, begin again at one. Losing count is simply a moment to return. You are not trying to perform a perfect exercise. You are giving your attention somewhere quiet and familiar to settle.
If the mind becomes busy, do not fight it. Notice one breath, one point of contact, and the rhythm of the massage.

Let the counting fall away now. Feel the breath without naming or measuring it. Notice the small release that may come with breathing out. It might be a softer shoulder, an easier hand, or simply less effort in listening.
Notice the base of your neck and the tops of your shoulders. On an easy out-breath, imagine those areas becoming wider. You do not have to move them; just reduce any unnecessary effort.

As the massage continues, let the breath and the touch be two gentle sensations in your awareness. They do not have to match. You can receive the touch while allowing your breathing to follow its own comfortable rhythm.
If you need to move or speak, you may. Your comfort matters throughout the session. Otherwise, allow yourself this quiet time to receive the massage.

If attention to breathing feels too busy, notice your hands resting instead. Feel the contact beneath them. Stay there for a moment. Breathing can look after itself while you give your mind this simpler place to rest.
Follow awareness down the arms, through the elbows, and into the hands. Let the fingers uncurl. Feel how little you need to do in order for your arms to remain supported.

Return to your breathing when you wish. Follow a quiet inhalation, then an easy exhalation. If it feels pleasant, allow the out breath to take a little more time. There is no need to empty your lungs completely.
Let the abdomen move naturally. There is nothing to hold in and nothing to force. Just an easy breath in, and a slower breath out.

Notice the support underneath your hips and legs. Imagine the surface receiving their weight with every exhalation. You need not push down. Let the feeling of being held replace a little of the effort of holding yourself.
Now soften the hips and thighs. Imagine the legs becoming heavier while the breath stays quiet and comfortable.

Bring the whole body into your awareness, breathing together. The face can soften, the chest can move, the abdomen can rest, and the legs can be supported. Allow these sensations to belong to one quiet moment.
Let awareness widen to include your whole body. Notice the head, the back, the arms, and the legs being supported at the same time. You can rest in that larger sense of contact.

Thoughts may still arrive. When you notice one, let it be there without following its next sentence. Feel one breath moving out. Then feel the contact beneath your body. Those two sensations can bring you back here.
If attention has wandered into a plan or a memory, notice that without criticism. Listen for one note in the music. Feel one point of support. You have already returned.

For this next breath, notice only the movement. For the breath after that, notice only the release. Then allow both to be present together, the body moving a little as you breathe, and resting a little as you exhale.

Let your breathing become as natural as possible. You do not have to deepen every breath. A small, comfortable breath can accompany a soft jaw, a relaxed belly, and the reassuring support underneath your body.
Take three easy breaths at your own pace. On each exhale, let go of tension that is no longer useful.

Sense whether there is one small area that would welcome less effort. Perhaps the fingers, the tongue, or the space between your shoulders. Breathe normally as that area softens by the amount that feels right for you.
Notice whether there is a small change in your jaw, hands, or shoulders. You do not need a dramatic result. A little less effort is enough; let that be the pace of this moment.

If your body begins to feel lighter, you may enjoy that lightness. If it feels pleasantly heavy, you may enjoy the support beneath it. There is no particular sensation you need to create. Let your own experience be enough.
Keep the jaw soft. Let the eyes rest. Feel the whole back of the body supported from head to heels.

Stay close to the simplicity of this moment. Breath coming in, breath moving out, body resting. Let each exhalation be a fresh invitation to soften. You can return to this quiet rhythm whenever your attention begins to wander.

Notice the beginning of an inhalation. Follow its movement without pulling in extra air. Notice the moment it turns into an exhalation. Follow that breath out, allowing the change of direction to happen by itself.
Follow the small movement of your breathing. Let it arrive naturally, without trying to fill your lungs or hold your breath. A comfortable breath is enough.

Notice where you feel this breath most clearly: around the nostrils, in the ribs, or in the belly. Let that simple sensation bring you back to the present.

Let this be enough for now: support beneath you, music around you, and one comfortable breath. Stay here without trying to improve the moment.

Scan from the forehead down through the chest and abdomen. Wherever you notice effort, invite a small amount of softness.

Return to your breathing when you wish. Follow a quiet inhalation, then an easy exhalation. If it feels pleasant, allow the out breath to take a little more time. There is no need to empty your lungs completely.
Let the shoulders, hands, belly and feet relax together. You do not need to make anything happen right now.

Notice the support underneath your hips and legs. Imagine the surface receiving their weight with every exhalation. You need not push down. Let the feeling of being held replace a little of the effort of holding yourself.

Notice the temperature of the room, the pressure of the massage, and the movement of your breath. Stay with those simple sensations.

Choose the part of the body that feels easiest to rest in. Stay there for a few comfortable breaths. It is fine if the feeling is subtle, ordinary, or different from what you expected.

Sense whether there is one small area that would welcome less effort. Perhaps the fingers, the tongue, or the space between your shoulders. Breathe normally as that area softens by the amount that feels right for you.
Notice whether there is a small change in your jaw, hands, or shoulders. You do not need a dramatic result. A little less effort is enough; let that be the pace of this moment.

Let the body remain at ease while you begin to notice the room around you. Feel the surface beneath you and listen to the sounds nearby. There is no need to move yet. Allow your breathing to stay comfortable.

Notice your hands and feet again. If it feels comfortable, make a small movement with your fingers or toes. Let your attention become a little wider, keeping the shoulders soft and taking your time to return.

Feel one comfortable breath come in, and let it leave gently. Notice the room, the support beneath you, and how your body feels. Open your eyes whenever you are ready. Move only when it suits you, slowly and with care.

Soften your shoulders and let your breath leave slowly. Take another breath at a comfortable pace. Imagine, if you like, a quiet place where you can rest. Let it be somewhere simple, with nothing you need to do.
Take a moment to adjust your position if you need to. Let your hands rest where they feel comfortable. Your eyes may close, or remain softly open. There is no right way to look relaxed.

You might picture a sheltered garden, with a comfortable place to lie beneath a light canopy. If another place feels more restful, choose that instead. You do not need a clear picture. A gentle sense of the place is enough.
There is no need to make the mind completely quiet. A thought can be present while the body rests. Let your next breath remind you that you can begin again, gently.

Imagine the air in this quiet place feeling pleasant against your skin. Let an easy breath come in, and let it leave. There is no need to breathe in time with my words. Allow yourself your own unhurried rhythm.
Follow the small movement of your breathing. Let it arrive naturally, without trying to fill your lungs or hold your breath. A comfortable breath is enough.

Perhaps there is soft daylight around you, neither too bright nor too dim. Notice one colour that feels restful. Let your mind rest with that colour while your body continues to feel the real support beneath it.
Notice several points where your body meets the table. Feel the fact that your weight is already being held for you.

Picture a broad path leading away from the place where you are resting. You do not need to walk along it. For now, you can stay where you are, allowing the demands of the day to remain somewhere beyond the path.
Imagine setting a small task down beside you for now. It will still be there later if it needs attention. In this moment, give yourself permission to receive support.

Listen for a gentle sound in your imagined place. It might be leaves moving, water in the distance, or a small bird far away. Let the sound be quiet and optional. The music around you can become part of that peaceful setting.
Let sounds come and go without following them. Each time attention wanders, return gently to one physical sensation.

With the next out breath, imagine a small ripple travelling across still water. Watch it spread and soften. Let the muscles around your eyes soften in the same unhurried way, without needing to make anything happen.
Bring awareness to the forehead and the small muscles around the eyes. Let the face become less busy. Allow a little space between the teeth and let the tongue rest easily.

Allow the garden, or your own chosen place, to have plenty of room. There is space for a thought to appear without taking over the whole scene. There is also space for your next breath, and for your body to rest.
If a thought arrives, let it pass like a sound in another room. Return to warmth, pressure and breathing.

Imagine a cloud passing slowly across a wide sky. You can notice its shape without needing to follow it. Let a thought pass in that same way. Then feel your next exhalation and the steady surface supporting you.
Bring attention to the chest and abdomen. Let the breath move through both areas without forcing depth.

Notice the comfortable place where you are lying in this imagined scene. Perhaps it is a soft cushion in the shade. Let that image remind your shoulders that they can rest, while the actual surface beneath you carries your weight.
Notice the base of your neck and the tops of your shoulders. On an easy out-breath, imagine those areas becoming wider. You do not have to move them; just reduce any unnecessary effort.

If pictures are not coming easily, let them go. Think of a simple word instead, perhaps spacious, or peaceful. Let that word pass quietly through your mind on an out breath. There is no need to repeat it perfectly.
On each exhale, imagine the body receiving one simple message: there is time, there is space, and you can soften now.

Imagine the light becoming gently warmer around your hands. You may notice real warmth, or only imagine it. Either is fine. Allow your fingers to remain loose, and let the muscles of your arms stop working quite so hard.
Bring attention to your hands. Uncurl the fingers and let the palms feel warm and loose.

Picture a leaf resting on the surface of a slow stream. There is no need to send it anywhere. Notice how it is carried without effort. Let the support beneath your body offer you something of that same ease.
Notice how much of your body can rest at the same time. Let the table support more of you than it did at the beginning.
If a task comes to mind, imagine placing its reminder on a bench beside the path. It will not be lost. You can return to it later. For this breath, your attention may come back to resting here.
If the mind becomes busy, do not fight it. Notice one breath, one point of contact, and the rhythm of the massage.

Let your imagined place become quieter in detail. Keep only what feels soothing: perhaps the soft light, the distant water, or the open space around you. The fewer things there are to arrange, the easier it may be to simply rest.
Let the hips and legs become heavy. Uncurl the toes. Release the hands. The body does not need to stay on alert.

As you breathe out, picture the surface of the water settling after a breeze. There is no requirement for your mind to become completely still. You can have thoughts and still allow your jaw, shoulders, and hands to soften.
Let the face, shoulders and abdomen soften together. Keep the exhale long enough to feel complete, but never strained.

Notice one comfortable sensation in your actual body. It may be warmth from the massage, the texture beneath your hand, or the quiet movement of breathing. Let this real sensation gently connect you with the peaceful scene you have imagined.
Choose the part of the body that feels easiest to rest in. Stay there for a few comfortable breaths. It is fine if the feeling is subtle, ordinary, or different from what you expected.

Imagine the edges of the garden opening into a wide, quiet landscape. There is room to breathe and no need to go anywhere. Let your exhalation feel like setting down a small burden you do not need to carry in this moment.
Feel the support beneath the back of your body. With each exhale, give a little more weight to the table.

If the image begins to fade, you do not have to rebuild it. Let it become only a feeling of space. Rest with your breathing and the contact below you. The quiet place can remain in the background without your effort.

Let your breath flow out gently, and allow your body to settle. Begin by softening your forehead and loosening your jaw. There is no need to tighten any muscles first. Let relaxation begin with a little less effort, right here.
You do not need to tense or stretch anything. Simply notice the weight of this part of your body. If something feels uncomfortable, tell your therapist and allow the position or pressure to change.

Feel the top of your head and the muscles around your scalp. You do not need to move them. Simply notice the area, then imagine its surface becoming a little softer as you take a comfortable breath out.
Start with the face and jaw. Smooth the forehead, soften the eyes, and let the lower jaw rest comfortably.

Bring attention to the space between your eyebrows. If there is a small crease there, let it ease by itself. Soften the corners of your eyes. You can keep your eyes open or closed, whichever helps you feel most comfortable.

Let your cheeks rest. Notice whether your teeth are pressing together, and allow a small space if that feels easy. Let your tongue settle naturally in your mouth. Breathe without trying to hold a particular expression on your face.
Bring awareness to the forehead and the small muscles around the eyes. Let the face become less busy. Allow a little space between the teeth and let the tongue rest easily.

Move your attention to the sides of your neck. Imagine the muscles becoming longer and easier, without stretching or moving your head. The support beneath your head can do its work while you let go of a little unnecessary effort.
Bring awareness to the neck and shoulders. As you breathe out, imagine the weight moving down and away from the ears.

Notice one shoulder, then the other. Rather than pushing them down, allow them to be supported. On your next exhalation, imagine each shoulder becoming a little broader, with more space around the muscles that have been holding it.
Notice the base of your neck and the tops of your shoulders. On an easy out-breath, imagine those areas becoming wider. You do not have to move them; just reduce any unnecessary effort.
Follow one arm from the shoulder towards the elbow. Let the upper arm be heavy enough to rest. Follow the other arm in the same way. There is no task for either arm to perform during this breath.
Follow awareness down the arms, through the elbows, and into the hands. Let the fingers uncurl. Feel how little you need to do in order for your arms to remain supported.

Feel the muscles around your wrists and the small spaces between your fingers. You do not have to open your hands deliberately. Allow any gripping to soften, even a little, while the breath moves in and out comfortably.
Bring attention to your hands. Uncurl the fingers and let the palms feel warm and loose.

Bring attention to your upper back. Imagine a tightly folded piece of cloth gently opening out. Let the muscles beside your shoulder blades have a little more room. You can receive the massage without needing to help those muscles move.
Let the upper back widen. Allow the shoulder blades to rest rather than hold themselves in position.

Notice your ribs and the natural movement around them. Breathing does not need to lift your shoulders. Let the ribs move in the way that suits your position, with an easy return as each breath flows out.
Move to the chest and ribs. Give the breath more room. Let the body expand on the inhale and settle on the exhale.
Allow the front of your body to rest as well. There is no need to pull your abdomen in or brace it. With the next exhalation, notice whether the centre of your body can feel a little less held.
Soften the abdomen. There is no need to brace. Let the centre of the body move naturally with each breath.

Bring your attention to your lower back. You are not trying to flatten or arch it. Let its natural shape be supported. Imagine the muscles on either side of your spine easing their effort as you breathe normally.
Notice the lower back and hips. Imagine the muscles spreading and releasing into the support underneath you.

Notice the area around your hips. If you have been holding yourself very still, allow a little permission to settle more comfortably. Let the surface below receive your weight. A small adjustment is welcome whenever you need it.
Notice the weight of the pelvis and the hips. Let the supporting surface meet that weight. Imagine that you have a little more room around the waist and across the back of the body.

Follow the length of one thigh, from the hip towards the knee. Imagine the broad muscles becoming soft and resting fully. Then follow the other thigh. Allow both legs to be present without having to keep them especially straight or still.
Let the thighs, knees and calves become heavy. Release any effort in the legs.

Notice the space around your knees. Let go of the idea that they need to be held in place. Follow your attention down through the calves, towards the ankles. With each breath, invite these muscles to do a little less.
Bring attention to the thighs, then the knees and calves. Let the legs be as heavy as they want to be. You do not need to straighten, stretch, or lift them.

Bring awareness to the soles of your feet and the tips of your toes. There is no need to point or stretch them. Imagine any small grip in the feet loosening, as though you had put down something you were carrying.
Relax the ankles, feet and toes. Then notice the hands and fingers. Let all four limbs feel loose at the same time.

Now move gently through the body again: face, shoulders, arms, back, hips, legs, and feet. You need not search for every trace of tension. Notice only the places that naturally draw your attention, and offer them a little softness.
Take a slow scan from head to feet. If you find a tense area, breathe toward it gently and create space around it.

Let a quiet breath come in. As it leaves, imagine the whole body becoming broader against its support. You may feel heaviness, lightness, or very little change. All of those experiences can belong to a moment of rest.
Take three quiet breaths. With each exhale, imagine the whole body becoming broader, heavier and softer.

If one area remains tense, leave some room around it. Relax the muscles nearby if that is easier. You can let the rest of your body soften without requiring that one area to change, and you can speak whenever you need an adjustment.
If you need to move or speak, you may. Your comfort matters throughout the session. Otherwise, allow yourself this quiet time to receive the massage.

Notice how relaxation can be small. A finger uncurling, a jaw unclenching, a shoulder resting a little more fully. Let these modest changes be enough. There is no need to force your body into a deeper or different feeling.
Notice whether there is a small change in your jaw, hands, or shoulders. You do not need a dramatic result. A little less effort is enough; let that be the pace of this moment.

Feel the outline of your whole body, supported from head to foot. Allow your next breath to be ordinary and easy. Let the muscles that can soften do so in their own time, while you remain comfortable and aware of the touch.

Follow one arm from the shoulder towards the elbow. Let the upper arm be heavy enough to rest. Follow the other arm in the same way. There is no task for either arm to perform during this breath.
Start with the face and jaw. Smooth the forehead, soften the eyes, and let the lower jaw rest comfortably.

Feel the muscles around your wrists and the small spaces between your fingers. You do not have to open your hands deliberately. Allow any gripping to soften, even a little, while the breath moves in and out comfortably.
Bring awareness to the neck and shoulders. As you breathe out, imagine the weight moving down and away from the ears.

Bring attention to your upper back. Imagine a tightly folded piece of cloth gently opening out. Let the muscles beside your shoulder blades have a little more room. You can receive the massage without needing to help those muscles move.
Let the upper back widen. Allow the shoulder blades to rest rather than hold themselves in position.

Notice your ribs and the natural movement around them. Breathing does not need to lift your shoulders. Let the ribs move in the way that suits your position, with an easy return as each breath flows out.
Move to the chest and ribs. Give the breath more room. Let the body expand on the inhale and settle on the exhale.
Allow the front of your body to rest as well. There is no need to pull your abdomen in or brace it. With the next exhalation, notice whether the centre of your body can feel a little less held.
Soften the abdomen. There is no need to brace. Let the centre of the body move naturally with each breath.

Bring your attention to your lower back. You are not trying to flatten or arch it. Let its natural shape be supported. Imagine the muscles on either side of your spine easing their effort as you breathe normally.
Notice the lower back and hips. Imagine the muscles spreading and releasing into the support underneath you.

Notice the area around your hips. If you have been holding yourself very still, allow a little permission to settle more comfortably. Let the surface below receive your weight. A small adjustment is welcome whenever you need it.
Let the thighs, knees and calves become heavy. Release any effort in the legs.

Follow the length of one thigh, from the hip towards the knee. Imagine the broad muscles becoming soft and resting fully. Then follow the other thigh. Allow both legs to be present without having to keep them especially straight or still.
Relax the ankles, feet and toes. Then notice the hands and fingers. Let all four limbs feel loose at the same time.

Notice the space around your knees. Let go of the idea that they need to be held in place. Follow your attention down through the calves, towards the ankles. With each breath, invite these muscles to do a little less.
Take a slow scan from head to feet. If you find a tense area, breathe toward it gently and create space around it.

Bring awareness to the soles of your feet and the tips of your toes. There is no need to point or stretch them. Imagine any small grip in the feet loosening, as though you had put down something you were carrying.
Allow the massage to do the work. Your job is simply to stay supported and let the body respond in its own time.

Now move gently through the body again: face, shoulders, arms, back, hips, legs, and feet. You need not search for every trace of tension. Notice only the places that naturally draw your attention, and offer them a little softness.
Take three quiet breaths. With each exhale, imagine the whole body becoming broader, heavier and softer.

Let a quiet breath come in. As it leaves, imagine the whole body becoming broader against its support. You may feel heaviness, lightness, or very little change. All of those experiences can belong to a moment of rest.
Notice the muscles around the ribs and lower back. Let them move with the breath instead of holding against it.

If one area remains tense, leave some room around it. Relax the muscles nearby if that is easier. You can let the rest of your body soften without requiring that one area to change, and you can speak whenever you need an adjustment.
Keep the sense of openness you have created. Easy breath, soft muscles and no unnecessary effort.

Notice how relaxation can be small. A finger uncurling, a jaw unclenching, a shoulder resting a little more fully. Let these modest changes be enough. There is no need to force your body into a deeper or different feeling.
You do not need to tense or stretch anything. Simply notice the weight of this part of your body. If something feels uncomfortable, tell your therapist and allow the position or pressure to change.

Feel the outline of your whole body, supported from head to foot. Allow your next breath to be ordinary and easy. Let the muscles that can soften do so in their own time, while you remain comfortable and aware of the touch.
Let the massage arrive at your own pace. You can soften a little without forcing a result. Notice the difference between holding yourself in place and allowing the table to support you.

Move your attention to the sides of your neck. Imagine the muscles becoming longer and easier, without stretching or moving your head. The support beneath your head can do its work while you let go of a little unnecessary effort.
Start with the face and jaw. Smooth the forehead, soften the eyes, and let the lower jaw rest comfortably.

Let the body remain at ease while you begin to notice the room around you. Feel the surface beneath you and listen to the sounds nearby. There is no need to move yet. Allow your breathing to stay comfortable.

Notice your hands and feet again. If it feels comfortable, make a small movement with your fingers or toes. Let your attention become a little wider, keeping the shoulders soft and taking your time to return.

Feel one comfortable breath come in, and let it leave gently. Notice the room, the support beneath you, and how your body feels. Open your eyes whenever you are ready. Move only when it suits you, slowly and with care.

Let yourself arrive here. Feel the surface underneath your body, and notice one easy breath moving in and out. You do not need to change what you feel. Begin simply by noticing where your body is resting at this moment.
Take a moment to adjust your position if you need to. Let your hands rest where they feel comfortable. Your eyes may close, or remain softly open. There is no right way to look relaxed.

Choose one clear point of contact, perhaps a hand, your back, or part of a leg. Notice whether the sensation is broad or small, warm or cool, light or firm. There is no correct answer to find. Just notice what is here.
Let attention rest on a sensation that feels neutral or comfortable. Notice its texture, warmth, or movement. You do not need to describe it perfectly; simply meet what is here.

Let your attention rest at that point of contact for another breath. If the sensation changes, notice the change. If it stays the same, notice its steadiness. You are not trying to hold a feeling in place or make it stronger.
You may notice that sensations change as you observe them. There is no need to chase the pleasant ones or push anything away. Stay curious, and return to the comfortable support beneath you.

Bring your awareness to your feet. You may notice the toes, the soles, or the surface supporting them. Perhaps the sensation is faint. Let faint sensations be faint, without needing to move or concentrate harder to discover something special.
Notice the heels, soles, and toes. Allow the feet to settle. Then sense the hands again, so that both your hands and your feet can rest together.

Allow attention to travel from your feet towards your ankles. Notice one side and then the other. Keep a sense of your breathing in the background, arriving and leaving naturally while you become familiar with this part of your body.

Move slowly into your lower legs. Feel whatever is available: contact, temperature, a sense of weight, or the position of your calves. You can also notice areas where the feeling is less clear. Nothing needs to be filled in.
Bring attention to the thighs, then the knees and calves. Let the legs be as heavy as they want to be. You do not need to straighten, stretch, or lift them.

Bring awareness to the knees. Rather than analysing them, feel their place within the whole leg. Let an easy exhalation pass. Then allow your attention to move towards the thighs, noticing the larger area of your body resting here.
Now soften the hips and thighs. Imagine the legs becoming heavier while the breath stays quiet and comfortable.

Notice your hips and the support beneath them. Feel the difference between the idea of your body and the actual sensations that are present now. You might notice warmth, pressure, or a gentle shift as you breathe.
Bring attention to the back and hips. There is nothing to judge. Simply notice sensation as it changes.

Let your attention move through the lower back. If the massage draws your awareness to a different place, it is fine to follow it for a moment. You can return to the lower back whenever that feels comfortable and useful.
Let attention settle around the middle and lower back. Notice the support there. If you find yourself bracing, invite just a little less effort, without demanding that the feeling disappear.

Notice the middle of your back, then the area around your shoulder blades. Let each region be known through simple sensation. There is no need to label it good or bad, relaxed or tense. Feel what you can, with a little curiosity.
Let the upper back widen. Allow the shoulder blades to rest rather than hold themselves in position.

Bring your awareness around to the movement of your ribs. Notice expansion and settling, however small they may be. Let one breath happen without changing it. Then notice the next breath as a new sensation, rather than an exact repeat.
Notice the chest and abdomen rising and settling. Let the breathing remain natural and unforced.

Feel your hands again, perhaps noticing a fingertip or the warmth of a palm. Compare the sensations in one hand and the other without deciding which is better. Allow both hands to rest while your attention moves gently between them.
Bring attention to your hands. Uncurl the fingers and let the palms feel warm and loose.

Travel along the wrists, forearms, and elbows. You may feel contact in one place and space around another. Notice those differences. Keep your attention light, as though you were listening carefully without needing to lean forward to hear.
Move attention through the shoulders and arms. Feel the difference between pressure, warmth and movement.

Bring awareness to your neck, then your jaw. Notice whether there is movement as you breathe, or a simple feeling of stillness. If the jaw naturally softens as you notice it, let that happen. If it does not, noticing is still enough.
Bring awareness to the forehead, jaw and neck. Notice what is present, then allow a small amount of softness.

Feel the skin of your face, the air around it, and the space around your eyes. You can soften your gaze or keep your eyes closed. Let your expression be easy, without needing to look as though you are relaxing.
Bring awareness to the forehead and the small muscles around the eyes. Let the face become less busy. Allow a little space between the teeth and let the tongue rest easily.

Now allow your attention to widen. Feel the body as a whole, rather than moving from one part to another. Breathing is happening somewhere within that larger field of sensation. The support underneath you is also present.
Let awareness widen to include your whole body. Notice the head, the back, the arms, and the legs being supported at the same time. You can rest in that larger sense of contact.

Notice a sound around you without searching for its source. Then feel one point of contact beneath your body. Then notice the movement of a breath. Move gently between these experiences, giving each a moment of simple attention.
Notice three sensations: the temperature of the air, the support of the table, and the touch of the massage.

If a thought carries you away, notice that you have remembered where you are. Feel your hand, your back, or another clear point of contact. Returning does not require an effortful correction. It can be as gentle as hearing the next note of music.
If attention has wandered into a plan or a memory, notice that without criticism. Listen for one note in the music. Feel one point of support. You have already returned.

See whether you can notice a sensation without adding a story to it. Warmth can simply be warmth. Movement can simply be movement. Let the experience be small and immediate, while your breathing continues at a comfortable pace.
Notice the temperature of the room, the pressure of the massage, and the movement of your breath. Stay with those simple sensations.

Include both the touch of the massage and the quieter sensations elsewhere in your body. You can let your awareness be broad, without concentrating on every detail. Speak if you need anything adjusted; being aware also means noticing your own comfort.
If you need to move or speak, you may. Your comfort matters throughout the session. Otherwise, allow yourself this quiet time to receive the massage.

Bring attention to one arm. Imagine it feeling pleasantly heavy, as though the surface beneath it were receiving all the weight it needs to receive. There is no need to press down or make the arm feel different. Simply offer the idea of rest.
Follow awareness down the arms, through the elbows, and into the hands. Let the fingers uncurl. Feel how little you need to do in order for your arms to remain supported.
